title: As Far from Land as Possible
prompt: Given an `n x n` grid containing only values `0` (water) and `1` (land), find a water cell such that its distance to the nearest land cell is maximized, and return that distance. Distance is measured using Manhattan distance (i.e., the minimum number of 4-directional steps between two cells). If no land or no water exists in the grid, return `-1`.

examples.explanation: The water cell (1,1) is 2 steps away from the nearest land, which is the maximum possible.
The cell (2,2) is farthest from the single land cell at (0,0), at Manhattan distance 4.
The grid is entirely land, so there is no water cell to measure a distance from, and the answer is -1.

hints: Running BFS separately from every water cell to find its nearest land would be far too slow — flip the direction of the search.
Use multi-source BFS starting from all land cells at once, expanding outward level by level, similar to rotting oranges or walls and gates.
The last level reached during this multi-source BFS (the final water cell visited) corresponds to the maximum distance to the nearest land; watch for the edge cases of an all-land or all-water grid.

solution.approach: Instead of searching from every water cell individually, start a multi-source BFS from every land cell simultaneously. Because BFS expands outward one distance-level at a time, the depth at which the last water cell is discovered equals the maximum possible distance from any water cell to its nearest land, since that farthest cell is by definition the last one any land-originated wave can reach. Return -1 immediately if the grid is all land or all water.
